MM inventory events on HYPE: Exp5 and Exp8

What two studies of the same ten HYPE market-maker wallets (MMs) found, and the evidence behind each claim. This is the opening overview of Exp8's full report, published on its own so it opens quickly; the report carries the same section plus its five detail sections and a 24-figure gallery. Figure and table numbers are the report's, so a number here points at the same panel or table there.

Exp5 spikes (revert)107
Exp5 cliffs (persist)168
Exp8 shocks (sudden)181
Window, both2025-03-27 → 2026-06-30
Detected on10 top-volume HYPE MMs
Exposure, both3,198 active wallet-days
Compared againstAll labeled HYPE MMs (median 249)
Evidence typeDescriptive, not causal

Overview: the two studies and what they found

The same ten HYPE market-maker MMs, the same fifteen months, and two deliberately different definitions of a sudden inventory event. Exp5 splits events by whether the position comes back — excursions that revert (spikes) against step changes that stay (cliffs). Exp8 asks only whether the move was sudden and large, and records what followed as a label. This section is what both found and the evidence behind it; sections A–H are Exp8 in full, and Exp5 has its own report.

The four things to take away. (1) The same ten HYPE market-maker wallets produce two distinct kinds of sudden inventory event — excursions that come back, and step changes that stay — and which kind an MM produces is a property of the MM, not of how much inventory it moves. (2) The events that come back are one-sided taker bursts absorbed on resting quotes, and they are absorbed by many MMs at once — never one. (3) Absorbing a burst and keeping it are different things: absorbing MMs hand back about 43 of every 100 HYPE they buy by the time the shock peaks, and getting the rest off takes hours — the median shocked MM still carries 38% of its excursion six hours later. (4) Nothing here is causal, and nothing here says the MMs trade badly: benchmarked against every other market maker trading the same side at the same moment, the shocked MM's execution is a coin flip.

Scope: what each study covers

Table 1 — Scope of the two studies, side by side. One row per design choice; the two columns are Exp5 (spikes and cliffs) and Exp8 (shocks). A cell spanning both columns is a choice the studies share.

Exp5 — spikes and cliffsExp8 — shocks
Question When an MM's inventory jumps within a day, does it come back? What do the two cases look like? When it jumps suddenly, what caused it, who else was hit, and how does the MM get out?
Detected on The same fixed roster of ten top-volume dominant HYPE market-maker wallets (the Exp7 roster; no new label join in either experiment).
Compared against The same ten. A separate scan covers 263 wallets, for rates only. Every wallet labeled a HYPE MM on the event date — a median 249 labeled, of which 95 clear the pre-event activity gate.
Window2025-03-27 → 2026-06-30 UTC, identical in both.
Exposure (the denominator) 3,198 active wallet-days — a date on which the wallet made ≥300 grouped fills and traded ≥$1m. Same screen in both, so the rates are comparable.
What is measured on The wallet's HYPE position in five-minute bins, rebuilt from its own fills, minus its trailing six-hour rolling median — divided by the wallet's own trailing robust scale σ (exact equations directly below this table). Every MM is judged against itself.
What counts as an event Spike: ≥8× the wallet's own normal deviation, ≥$100k, peak reached within 25 minutes, and it returns — retraces at least half, comes back through a narrow band on both sides, and leaves no lasting level change.
Cliff: the mirror image — a 5-to-60-minute one-way move of ≥6× the wallet's own scale, with ≥70% of it still there one hour and two hours later.		 Shock: ≥6× the wallet's own normal deviation measured on a trailing 7-day scale, ≥$100k, with 60% of the build inside a single 25-minute stretch, and prominent: the peak's distance from the trailing median is at least 1.5× the largest such distance the wallet showed in the 3 hours before the window (and, if the position comes back, in the 3 hours after). Prominence compares the size of the move with the size of the wallet's other recent moves, not with the size of its book (rule 10 below). Whether it comes back is not part of the rule — it is recorded afterwards as a label (revert / partial / step).
Events found 107 spikes and 168 cliffs 181 shocks (125 up, 56 down)
Rate 3.35 spikes and 5.25 cliffs per 100 active wallet-days 5.66 shocks per 100 active wallet-days
How precision was established Panels read one at a time, one verdict each, across five detector versions: ~95% of spikes and 97.6% of cliffs judged genuine (164 true, 1 drift, 3 ambiguous, 0 mislabelled spikes). Same instrument: 92.2% — 59 true of 64 panels, drawn at random in two independent draws (40 at one seed, 24 at another).
Per-fill attribution available Yes for spikes — flow, execution, markouts. None at all for cliffs. Yes — population absorption, unwind paths, peer-benchmarked execution, and exact counterparty pairing (the latter only up to 2025-11-24).
Kind of evidence Descriptive association on a five-minute grid. Neither experiment establishes cause.

The exact construction

For one wallet at five-minute bin t (all quantities are per-wallet), with position Pt in HYPE and mid price mt:

devt  =  Pt − median(Pt−72, …, Pt−1) trailing 6-hour median: 72 bins, ≥36 valid — centers the position at the wallet's own current level

σ7dt  =  1.4826 × median( |devs| : s an active-day bin in the trailing 7 days ) 2,016 bins, ≥288 valid — a robust (MAD) spread of the deviation; sets the unit

σt  =  max( σ7dt,  0.02 × p95(|P|)30d,  $12,500 / mt ) p95 of |position| over the trailing 30 days, lagged one day so it never sees the shock

zt  =  devt / σt ,   shock candidate when |zt| ≥ 6

z is a robust z-score: the deviation is measured from a median rather than a mean, and scaled by a median absolute deviation (MAD) rather than a standard deviation, so one wild bin cannot inflate its own yardstick. A shock must pass every rule below, in this order. Each bullet says what the rule is for and what it excludes.

  1. Centering — trailing 6-hour median (72 bins, at least 36 valid). devt is the position minus the median of the six hours before t. A wallet that carries a large book all day has a large median and a small deviation; the level of the book is never what is being tested.
  2. Scale — trailing 7-day MAD of the deviation. σ7dt is how big this wallet's ordinary wobble has been over the last week of active days, so a $500k move is a shock for a wallet that usually wobbles by $50k and nothing for one that usually wobbles by $500k.
  3. Denominator floor 1 — σt is never below $12,500 of HYPE. Guards against dividing by almost zero. A wallet whose position barely moved for a week has a MAD near zero and would register a shock on a one-coin rounding change. Since a candidate needs 6σ, this floor implies a minimum move of $75k, below the $100k size rule, so it never acts as a second size rule. It sets σt for 3 of the 181 shocks.
  4. Denominator floor 2 — σt is never below 2% of the wallet's 30-day p95 |position| (lagged one day). For wallets that are quiet but big: a $300k move on a $6m book is many MADs if the book has been calm, but is 5% of the book and not a shock for that MM. Sets σt for 5 of the 181; removing this floor adds 2 candidate events.
  5. Candidate — |zt| ≥ 6 on an active wallet-day. The wallet's position is six of its own ordinary wobbles away from its own six-hour level. An active wallet-day has at least 300 grouped fills and $1m traded.
  6. Observed start — walking back from the peak, |z| falls to 1.5 within 3 hours without crossing a data gap. Excludes excursions whose beginning is missing, because every later measurement (formation time, speed, cause) needs the start.
  7. Size — |devpeak| × mid ≥ $100k. A dollar floor on the move itself, so a small book cannot produce a shock out of a few thousand dollars, however many MADs that is.
  8. Suddenness — 60% of the build inside one 25-minute stretch (v2, this catalogue). Separates a jump from a drift. Section B3 shows this rule scales with the event's own size and rejects large slow builds; the v3 velocity rule is the replacement candidate.
  9. Straight, traded build-up — path efficiency ≥ 0.5 and fills in at least half the formation bins. Excludes zig-zag paths and carried-forward flat positions that only look like a move because the wallet stopped trading.
  10. Prominence — |devpeak| ≥ 1.5 × the largest |dev| in the 3 hours before the window; for events whose level comes back, also ≥ 1.5 × the largest |dev| in the 3 hours after. Both sides compare deviations from the trailing median, not positions, so a large standing inventory does not disqualify anything: the 181 shocks start from pre-window median books between $0.5k and $20.6m (25% above $444k). What it does exclude is a big move that is not alone: a second swing within three hours of a first one of similar size, or a wallet that oscillates by this much routinely, so a cluster of equally large shocks can yield none. This is the costliest rule in the funnel: it cuts 737 candidate windows to 217 (v2, 6-hour baseline), and at a multiplier of 1.0 the catalogue would be 383 shocks instead of 181, the extra events concentrated in ranks 2 (46→132) and 7 (16→59), the two constantly oscillating wallets. Those 202 were never audited by eye, so recall on clustered shocks is a known cost, not a measured one (tables/shock_threshold_sensitivity.csv, tables/detection_funnel.csv).
  11. Live wallet at the start — fills in at least half the bins of the prior 2 hours, and both a buy and a sell in the prior 6 hours. Excludes a dormant wallet whose first fill of the day reads as a jump.

Whether the position comes back is not a rule. It is recorded afterwards as a label (revert / partial / step) from the residual level shift 60 minutes after the window. The exact role of the two floors, and how often each one is the term that sets σt, is below.

How far the peak stands from the level the wallet held before the shock. One row of the underlying data is one of the 181 shocks. Definitions:

  • Pre-shock level — the median of the wallet's 5-minute position over the 60 minutes before the window opens; the same level the revert / partial / step label is judged against.
  • Amplitude — |position at the peak − pre-shock level|. This is the "peak compared to the previous median" quantity. It is reported instead of a ratio of the two positions because 103 of the 181 shocks cross zero (the peak has the opposite sign to the pre-shock level), which makes a ratio of levels meaningless; the ratio row divides the amplitude by the pre-shock |position| instead.
  • Detection deviation — |position − trailing 6-hour median| at the peak bin, the quantity the detector thresholds (Table 2, row C); shown so the two "distance from level" measures can be compared. They agree closely because the 60-minute and 6-hour medians sit at nearly the same level before a shock.
  • Own volume — the wallet's own HYPE fill volume in dollars per 5-minute bin, maker and taker, buy and sell. Pre-window is the 6 hours (72 bins) before the window opens, summarized by its median bin; formation is window start to peak (median 10 minutes); whole window is start to end. The two ratio rows have N = 180 because one shock has a pre-window median volume of zero.

Equity and effective leverage around each shock (Table 5). Leverage is measured per fill: lev = k × 2 × max leverage, where k = maintenance margin / pool equity from the per-fill k dataset and HYPE's max leverage is 10 throughout the sample — so liquidation sits at 20× (k = 1); exact at the base maintenance tier. The value at a reference time is taken just after the MM's last HYPE fill at or before it, 60-minute lookback (per-fill data 2025-09-27 onward → 99 of the 181 shocks). Equity is the exchange account checkpoint series (cadence ~2 h in 2025, ~5.5 h by mid-2026), so the three reference points are: the last checkpoint before the window opens (≤8 h back), the first checkpoint after the peak (≤6 h), and the first checkpoint after peak+6 h (≤14 h) — checkpoint equity, not a 5-minute path:

The stronger fact is selection: during shock windows effective leverage runs at 2.3× its all-times median (0.65× vs 0.28×) — shocks happen when MMs are already running more levered — yet even the in-shock p75 (1.68×) sits a factor of twelve from the 20× liquidation boundary.

Who: the ten roster MMs only, not the wider MM population. Grain: one value per wallet per UTC day, the last snapshot of that day, so N = 2,641 is wallet-days: 268 to 277 days for nine wallets and 195 for rank 7, over the 277 days 2025-09-27 → 2026-06-30 where the snapshot feed exists (99 of the 181 shocks fall inside it). Within a day the snapshot cadence is ~2 h in 2025 degrading to ~5.5 h by mid-2026. Zero-value snapshots are exchange-reported (emptied accounts), kept as recorded. Per-wallet rows are in the appendix.

Per-wallet versions of every panel are in appendix J2.

Both catalogues are frozen, and both precision figures are counts of human verdicts on rendered panels, not estimates from a model. That is the reason to trust the event lists at all.

What Exp5 observed: two families of event

  • Two families of event, and they sort the MMs. A spike reverts; a cliff stays. Ranks 6 and 8 produce zero spikes and 34 cliffs between them; ranks 2, 7 and 10 produce 54 spikes and 1 cliff; rank 1 does both (28 spikes, 97 cliffs). Rates over the same 3,198 active wallet-days (Exp5 §E). In the wider cohort of 263 dominant-MM wallets: 4.34 spikes and 8.33 cliffs per 100 wallet-days, and 49% of wallets produce neither (Exp5 §F).
  • A spike is absorbed flow, later unwound. Many takers converge on one side within a few minutes, the MM takes the other side on resting quotes, and the position is worked back to its level (Exp5 §C1).
  • The cost is in the move that follows. Volume-weighted maker markout 60 minutes out: −1.41 bps on spike-window fills against +1.73 bps on the same wallets' other fills that day (both excluding 2025-10-10, which alone is −118.53 bps); up-spikes +2.50, down-spikes −9.08. An earlier positive estimate was an artifact of a 25-minute build cap and is corrected in Exp5 §C3.
  • A cliff is a re-targeted book. Median $1.54m moved in 50 minutes and kept; 72 of 168 flip the sign of the position outright; 105 up, 63 down (Exp5 §D).
Figure 2 — what a cliff looks like (Exp5), for the side-by-side with Figure 1

What Exp8 observed: cause, absorption, unwind

  • A shock is a one-sided taker burst, not a busy market. Over the 181 shocks, taker volume on the side trading against the MM runs at a median 5.29× its trailing 24-hour rate; some hit-side surge is present in 92.8% of shocks and exceeds 2× in 82.9%; taker imbalance toward that side is +0.443 and the flow is one-sided in 87.8%. Both sides accelerate — in the three episodes measured minute by minute the hit side runs 6.4× / 27.3× / 60.3× against 3.7× / 14.0× / 34.3× for total volume. Everything sped up, and the side hitting the MM sped up far more (§C).
  • Takers sell into these MMs about twice as often as they buy. 125 up shocks against 56 down (§C).
  • No shock is absorbed alone. The burst on the shock side is met by a median of 71 absorbing wallets out of 95 active MMs. The denominator decides this: over the ten roster wallets only the shocked MM holds 60–77% of same-side movement, but against every active MM the largest single MM holds 23–36% and the ten together 36–47%. "It absorbed this alone" is what a ten-wallet denominator looks like (§D).
  • Most shocked MMs are outside the detected ten. In the three detailed episodes, 9 of 13, 10 of 13 and 26 of 31 MMs hit for 3× their own scale were not roster members. Shocked MMs are almost always shocked on the same side as the event; the crash day is the exception — 10 of 41 were shocked the other way, a two-sided cascade (§D1).
  • Getting out is slow and often incomplete. Aligning every shocked MM on its own peak and scaling by its own excursion: the median still carries 38% of it six hours later, only 61% ever get three-quarters back, and the 75th-percentile path sits at exactly 1.00 for the full six hours — a quarter of shocked MMs simply keep the position. Shocked MMs outside the ten are slower still (median 0.56 at six hours), so reading recovery speed off ten large MMs overstates how fast this population gets flat (§E1).
  • Execution during the unwind is unremarkable, and that is a finding. Every number here is benchmarked against every MM trading the same side, in the same 60 minutes, off the same reference price.
    • Price against its own peak mid: +16.2 bps; peer median +18.3. The sign is corrected for shock direction, so + means better than flattening at the peak whether the wallet was selling down a long or buying back a short. Split out it is +23.0 bps on the 124 up shocks and −9.4 bps on the 56 down shocks: the pooled level averages two opposite price regimes, which is why only the benchmarked gap is interpretable (§E2).
    • 30-minute markout: −7.6 bps; peer median −8.8.
    • 60-minute markout: −15.3 bps; peer median −10.7.
    • Like for like, the gap is 0.4 bp on price and 1.0 bp on both markouts, putting the shocked MM at the 46th to 49th percentile of its peers. Those gaps are medians of the per-shock paired difference, so by construction they are not the difference of the two medians listed above.
    • A negative markout is the normal condition here, not a symptom: that side of that window paid everybody.
    • MMs that got flat fast printed far worse absolute prices, −76.9 bps against the peak mid versus +8.2 bps for MMs that sat still. That gap is where each wallet's own peak happened to sit on the price path, not how well it traded: inside each pilot episode the price metric is 0.85 to 0.89 rank-correlated with the wallet's own peak-bin mid, and the fast wallets' 60-minute markout is no worse than the slow wallets' (§E2).
  • Unwinding is a post-only activity. Across the 181 shocks the ten MMs unwind with post-only limit orders (84.4% of volume on average, 97.9% median) and immediate-or-cancel orders (14.3% average) — 98.7% together, and not once with a scheduled time-weighted order or a frontend market order. Two of the ten are exceptions and cross the spread routinely (one for 80% of its unwind volume). The concession is in where quotes sit, not in crossing the spread (§E2).
  • Market makers are a large share of each other's flow. From exact counterparty pairing, when an MM crosses the spread during these events 20.9% / 41.1% / 64.2% of that volume is taken from another MM's resting quote across the three episodes. Shocked-MM-to-shocked-MM volume is negligible in normal conditions ($0.08m) and $2.10m on the crash day — under stress they do unload into each other, though the data cannot separate that from "peers were simply the resting liquidity" (§D2).

Why there are two catalogues, and how they overlap

The two definitions are deliberately different, and the catalogues overlap without either containing the other. At its operating threshold Exp8 keeps 55.1% of Exp5's 107 spikes and 18.5% of its 168 cliffs. Three reasons, all mechanical:

  • The yardstick changed, which matters more than the threshold number looks. Exp8 measures each move against the wallet's trailing seven-day scale, and that scale runs about 1.8× the full-sample scale precisely at event times. So Exp8's "6×" is a stricter test than Exp5's "8×", despite the smaller number.
  • Most cliffs fail the suddenness rule. 46% of cliffs sit exactly at Exp5's 60-minute ceiling, and a 60-minute one-way move can place at most about 42% of itself inside any 25-minute stretch, against Exp8's 60% requirement.
  • Exp8 refuses to put the outcome in the definition. Its step class is conceptually a cliff and its revert class conceptually a spike; it labels what happened afterwards instead of gating on it. Exp5 asks "did the MM absorb and return, or re-target?", which needs the outcome in the rule; Exp8 asks "how often does inventory move suddenly, whatever follows?", which needs it out. Neither framing is more correct.

What neither study establishes

Both studies are descriptive. What follows bounds what can be said from them; §H carries Exp8's full list, including its two known data defects.

  • Nothing is causal. A taker burst and an inventory build occupying the same ten minutes is an association on a five-minute grid, not a demonstrated cause.
  • Detection is on ten wallets in both studies. Events where only other market makers were hit are invisible, and there are no event counts or rates for anyone outside the ten: Exp5's 263-wallet scan gives rates only, and Exp8's population work is all measured inside windows the ten defined.
  • Counts are concentrated in a few MMs. Rank 2 is 41 of 107 spikes; rank 1 is 97 of 168 cliffs; two wallets are 99 of 181 shocks and three contribute 6 between them. Any per-wallet cell in single digits is indicative only.
  • Precision is 92–98%, not 100%, and the residual failures are recorded rather than tuned away: small events in wallets that oscillate constantly, and events whose peak sits hours after the fast move.
  • In sections A–E, quoting is only observed where a quote was filled. Every "spread" figure there is a realized, fill-conditional price gap. NEW The raw order stream (posts, cancels, resting prices) turned out to be available on this host (2026-09-03); its first use is §G, and nothing before that section has been rebuilt on it.
  • Cliffs have no attribution at all. Whether they are informed repositioning or forced unwinding is untested — the obvious next experiment.
  • 2025-10-10 is a distinct regime — 41% of its formation flow is forced liquidation or auto-deleveraging, and markout magnitudes are an order of magnitude larger. It is reported separately throughout and must not be pooled.
  • Slow permanent re-targeting is out of scope by construction in both detectors. An MM that moves inventory slowly registers zero events, and one of the ten does exactly that. Zero means "no sudden change", never "no inventory change".
If you are presenting this: a 15-minute running order

Table 6 — A 15-minute running order for presenting the two studies. One row per minute block: what to put up and the one point to make.

minWhat to put upThe one point
0–2the scope table above Same ten MMs, same 15 months, same 3,198 active wallet-days, two deliberately different event definitions. Every MM is judged against itself.
2–4Figure 1, then Figure 4 This is what an event is, and this is the panel a human read one at a time to get 92–98% precision. The catalogues are audited, not assumed.
4–7Figures 1 and 2 side by side, then the per-wallet rate table above Two families, and they sort the MMs. Ranks 6 and 8: zero spikes, 34 cliffs. Rank 2: 41 spikes, 1 cliff.
7–9Figure 3 Inside a spike: takers hit a resting quote, inventory jumps, it is worked back. Mention the +3.69 bps composition trap and the 2025-10-10 markout split — both are places this project corrected itself.
9–12Figure 6 and the denominator callout in §D Who else was there. A median 71 absorbing wallets out of 95 active MMs, so the denominator decides every share; and the regime split — labeled MMs absorbed 70% and 90% of the burst in the two normal episodes but only 10% of the $528m crash-day burst.
12–14Figure 8 and the table in §E2 Getting out is slow (38% still carried at six hours, a quarter keep it outright) and execution is a coin flip against peers. Slow is not the same as bad.
14–15What neither study establishes, above No causality, ten detected wallets, cliffs unattributed, 2025-10-10 separate. The open test: attribute cliffs, and detect on the population rather than on ten MMs.

If the slot is 20 minutes rather than 15, the two places worth the extra time are the D1 ladder (why one number was compared with another it should never have been compared with, and what the like-for-like answer is) and the two-catalogues note above (why two catalogues exist at all). Neither needs a new figure.
